summary: Proposes improvements to unicast Reverse Path Forwarding for detecting and reducing source address spoofing. It explains why strict, loose, and the existing feasible-path uRPF still have shortcomings and describes an enhanced approach. It relates to RFC 3704 and BCP 38.

eli5.summary: Spoofers write fake return addresses. Routers can check whether a letter could really have come from where it claims, and this does that more carefully.

questions: how to prevent source address spoofing
strict vs loose vs feasible-path urpf
subtitle: A smarter source-address check for ISP edge routers that drops spoofed packets without dropping customers' real traffic.

tldr.problem: Existing uRPF checks either wrongly drop legitimate customer packets (strict and feasible-path) or ignore which interface a packet should arrive on (loose), so ISPs hesitate to deploy them.
tldr.mechanism: Enhanced feasible-path uRPF builds each customer interface's list of permitted source prefixes from all BGP routes that share the same origin AS, whichever interface the routes arrived on.
tldr.outcome: It sharply reduces false positives while keeping directionality, which is meant to encourage wider deployment of source address validation. It is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 3704.

today: RFC 8704 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 84) that updates RFC 3704, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Source Address Validation Needs Better uRPF
sections.content:
Source address validation (SAV) means detecting and mitigating source address spoofing, as described in BCP 38 (RFC 2827). Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF), defined in RFC 3704, is one way to do it. Strict uRPF is inflexible about directionality, loose uRPF ignores directionality, and feasible-path uRPF tries to balance the two but still has shortcomings.

Even with feasible-path uRPF, ISPs often worry that they may be dropping customers' packets that carry legitimate source addresses. This document proposes enhanced feasible-path uRPF (EFP-uRPF) to be more flexible about directionality in a meaningful way, and so to ease those worries and encourage more deployment.

The RFC assumes the routes in use have already been vetted by prefix filtering (RFC 7454) and possibly origin validation (RFC 6811).
sections.eli5: Routers can check where a packet says it came from. The old checks are either too picky and toss good packets, or too relaxed and let fakes in. This makes the check smarter.

sections.title: The Existing Techniques and Their Limits
sections.content:
SAV is performed at network edge devices such as border routers, cable modem termination systems and mobile packet data network gateways. The RFC reviews five approaches.

  • Access control lists list acceptable or unacceptable source prefixes, but updating them is a manual operator process, so keeping them current is operationally difficult or infeasible.
  • Strict uRPF accepts a packet only if the FIB has a prefix covering the source address and that prefix points back out the interface the packet arrived on. It fails with multihoming and asymmetric routing.
  • Feasible-path uRPF also adds prefixes from alternative announced routes to the RPF list. It works only if announcements propagate to all transit providers, and it can still fail, for example when a provider prefers a shorter route via a lateral peer over a longer customer route and so never announces the prefix onward.
  • Loose uRPF only checks that the FIB has some route for the source address, so it sacrifices directionality and drops only unreachable sources.
  • VRF tables let the uRPF check query a dedicated per-peer table instead of the FIB, giving strict-like behavior, or a global table for loose behavior.
sections.eli5: There are several ways to check return addresses. Some are too strict and reject real mail from a customer who uses two post offices. Others only check that the address exists somewhere.

sections.title: The EFP-uRPF Algorithms
sections.content:
The core principle: if BGP updates for multiple prefixes with the same origin AS were received on different interfaces at border routers, then packets with source addresses in any of those prefixes should be accepted on any of those interfaces. In the RFC's example, a border router knows prefixes Q1, Q2 and Q3, all originated by AS-x in its customer cone. Q1 came from a customer, Q2 from a lateral peer and Q3 from an upstream provider, yet all three go into the RPF list of the customer interface.

Algorithm A groups prefixes by origin AS. It takes the unique origin ASes seen on customer interfaces, forms for each the set of unique prefixes with that origin across all interfaces, and puts that set in the RPF list of every customer interface where at least one of its prefixes was received.

Algorithm B adds flexibility across the customer cone. It takes all unique prefixes from customer interfaces (Set P) and all prefixes from lateral peer and transit provider interfaces whose origin AS is among the customer origin ASes (Set Q). The union of P and Q is the RPF list for every customer interface.

Algorithm B is needed in a challenging scenario in which a customer announces prefixes to one provider with NO_EXPORT, so the upstream never sees them on that interface. Algorithm A fails there and Algorithm B works, with directionality only minimally compromised, which is still much better than loose uRPF.
sections.eli5: If a router sees addresses from the same sender arriving by different roads, it remembers they all belong to that sender. Then a letter from any of those addresses is fine on any of those roads that lead to that sender.

sections.title: Operational Recommendations and ROA Data
sections.content:
To keep EFP-uRPF robust, a multihomed stub AS should announce at least one of its originated prefixes to each of its transit providers. A non-stub AS should do the same, and in addition SHOULD announce at least one route per origin AS, from the routes learned from customers, to each of its transit providers.

RPF lists can also be augmented from secondary sources. If a Route Origin Authorization (RFC 6482) includes a prefix and an AS, the prefix is added to the RPF list of the customer interfaces involved. Reliable IRR data can be used the same way, but the RFC warns that IRR data is not always accurate or trusted.

Routes can be withdrawn and reannounced briefly, for example after a BGP session reset or link failure recovery. Deleting entries from RPF lists SHOULD therefore be delayed by a predetermined amount based on operational experience, to suppress these transients.
sections.eli5: Customers should tell every one of their providers at least some of their addresses. And when an address briefly disappears, the router should wait a bit before forgetting it.

sections.title: Memory Cost on Line Cards
sections.content:
Unlike the normal FIB, an EFP-uRPF list is built from all received BGP routes, not only the best path. Line cards must therefore accept arbitrary RPF lists, stored in TCAM. The list size per line card will roughly equal the number of prefixes originated in the ISP's customer cone when Algorithm B is used. Algorithm A needs much less memory.

The RFC cites measured customer cone sizes: 32393 prefixes for a very large global ISP, 20038 for a large global ISP, 8661 for a mid-size global ISP and 1101 for a regional ISP in Asia. It compares these with FIB capacities of about 2 million, 1 million, 0.5 million and 100k routes, and concludes the RPF list is only a small fraction of the FIB. It also notes that uRPF is most effective at the edges of the Internet, where customer cones are smaller.
sections.eli5: The router needs a bigger notebook to keep these lists. The RFC counted and found that even a small router has plenty of room for it.

sections.title: Recommendations and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The summary of recommendations depends on the scenario:

  • For directly connected networks, SHOULD perform ACL-based SAV.
  • For a directly connected single-homed stub AS, SHOULD use strict uRPF.
  • In all other cases, SHOULD apply EFP-uRPF with Algorithm B on customer interfaces and loose uRPF on lateral peer and transit provider interfaces.
  • Prefixes from registered ROAs and IRR route objects for ASes in the customer cone SHOULD augment the RPF lists.

Algorithm A is only an alternative. It is expected to work if an ISP has only multihomed stub customers, and is equal to strict uRPF for a single-homed stub customer. It is risky because an ISP may not be able to track how much NO_EXPORT is used in its customer cone.

The security considerations of BCP 38 and RFC 3704 apply. Augmenting lists with ROA data trades fewer false positives for a slight risk that a malicious actor elsewhere in the customer cone could use the augmented prefix. That risk is mitigated if the other AS's transit provider performs SAV. Routers and supporting systems such as RPKI and ROA management must also be hardened against compromise.
sections.eli5: The guide says which check to use where: strict for simple customers, the smarter one for most others. The small risk is that a sneaky neighbor might borrow an address that was added to the list.
